planting.note: Plant container stock in spring in acidic, humus-rich, well-drained soil in dappled shade; this is a naturally occurring floral-form variant rather than a bred color selection, so propagate from cuttings or grafts of known plants rather than seed.

directions: This long-recognized botanical form of mountain laurel departs from the species' typical bowl-shaped bloom: instead of a fused cup, each corolla splits into five narrow, separate strap-like petals, giving the open flower a feathery, spidery look quite unlike any color-based cultivar. Flower buds often look slightly irregular or untidy before opening, which is normal for this form and not a sign of poor health. Site it exactly as you would any mountain laurel, in acidic, well-drained, humus-rich soil with consistent moisture and protection from hot afternoon sun. Because the trait is structural rather than a named breeding achievement, plants sold under this name are propagated vegetatively from an original selection to keep the split-petal form true. All parts of the plant are toxic if ingested.
sources: Journal of the American Rhododendron Society (Jaynes, 'The Kalmias and Their Hybrids')

planting.note: Plant container stock in spring in acidic, humus-rich, well-drained soil in dappled shade; this slow, dense dwarf form has been in cultivation since the 1880s and is propagated from cuttings of known plants to preserve its small leaf and compact habit.

directions: One of the oldest recognized dwarf forms of mountain laurel, myrtifolia keeps leaves noticeably smaller and narrower than the species, pointed and leathery like true myrtle foliage, packed densely along slow-growing stems. Its flowers are pale pink, opening from slightly darker pink buds, in smaller clusters scaled to match the reduced leaf size. The tight, slow-growing habit tops out at a fraction of the species' size, making it a good fit for a small shaded border or rock-garden-adjacent planting where a full-size mountain laurel would quickly overwhelm the space. Grow it exactly as you would any mountain laurel: acidic, humus-rich, well-drained soil, steady moisture, and protection from harsh afternoon sun. All parts of the plant are toxic if ingested.
sources: Journal of the American Rhododendron Society (Jaynes, 'The Kalmias and Their Hybrids')

planting.note: Plant container stock in spring in acidic, humus-rich, well-drained soil; Sepulga Pink traces to wild populations along Alabama's Sepulga River and tolerates more sun and summer heat than most mountain laurel selections.

directions: Named for the Sepulga River region of south Alabama where its parent plants were found, this selection was chosen for performing well in the hot, humid summers of the Deep South, a climate that stresses many northern-bred mountain laurel cultivars. It grows into a full, rounded shrub reaching roughly five to seven feet, bearing bright pink buds that open to flowers blending pink and white across each bloom. Give it more sun than a typical mountain laurel would tolerate, since its Gulf Coast heritage makes it noticeably more heat- and humidity-tolerant, though it still wants acidic, well-drained, humus-rich soil and should not be allowed to dry out completely. It is a good choice for warm-climate woodland gardens from the mid-Atlantic through the Gulf South where straight K. latifolia often struggles. All parts of the plant are toxic if ingested.
